claims.text: The unusual high-temperature strength retention of refractory high-entropy alloys arises from edge-dislocation-controlled deformation.
Multi-element mixing creates large local lattice distortions that elevate the activation energy for edge dislocation motion.
The thermoelastic behavior of refractory high-entropy alloys arises from the elevated barrier to edge dislocation motion.
When impurity-induced phase segregation is minimized, a stable edge-dislocation network dominates plastic flow.
When impurity-induced phase segregation is minimized, a stable edge-dislocation network dominates thermal response.
NbTaTiV and CrMoNbV are applicable examples of BCC refractory high-entropy alloys for the proposed comparison.
Low levels of interstitial impurities such as oxygen and nitrogen can promote phase segregation during thermal exposure.
The proposed mechanism applies over 800°C to 1000°C.
An inert atmosphere avoids oxidation during the high-temperature comparison.
Edge-dislocation density, configuration, and mobility mediate the mechanical response.
The increased energy barrier for edge dislocation motion preserves high-temperature strength.
The increased energy barrier for edge dislocation motion stabilizes thermoelastic properties at high temperature.
Impurity-driven segregation depletes strengthening interstitial solutes from the matrix and produces progressive softening during aging.
Impurity-driven segregation reduces solute-mediated edge-dislocation pinning.
Ultra-high-purity alloys will retain higher high-temperature yield strength than impurity-doped alloys of the same composition.
Ultra-high-purity alloys will exhibit more stable elastic moduli and less thermoelastic softening than impurity-doped alloys.
Ultra-high-purity alloys will retain a higher-density, less-mobile edge-dislocation network than impurity-doped alloys.
The proposed mechanism is expected to be dominant specifically in single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloys and may differ when phase transitions or oxidation occur.
